title:
A deck you can
keep working on.
pages.notes: I want to start with why this exists, not with a feature list. I make slides constantly — group meeting, lab presentations, talks. Over the last year I became convinced that agents will write slides the way they now write code and text. The question I care about is not whether they can, but whether the result can sound like a person. This is the story of the two or three things that got in the way, and the editor I built around them.

title: One project. One writer. Any assistant.
pages.notes: This began in group meeting. Someone would put up a deck, and my advisor — and honestly most of the room — could tell almost immediately that a model had made it. The design was often fine. Sometimes it was better than fine. The tell was that nobody seemed to have chosen anything. I started watching for that feeling instead of for a particular template.

designIntent.purpose: Define the product in one page: one project, one writer, any assistant; explain the Editor/project/plugin/connector relationship.
keep: Concept diagram, not a fake screenshot
Client marks identify routes, not endorsements

visibleText: One project. One writer. Any assistant.
HUANDENG is a desktop editor for presentations that keep changing. The slides live in a project folder; you and your AI assistant write through the same page-oriented service.
The Editor is where you edit. The plugin or connector is how an assistant reaches it. The project folder is the document; moving it moves the deck.
Concept diagram. Client marks identify supported routes; ChatGPT connects through the authorized workstation.

title: The texture is not a style. It is an absence of focus.
pages.notes: The usual explanation is AI style — a font, a gradient, a layout. I don't think that's it. The deck I recognized was complete in a way a person rarely is. Every point had a slide; every slide had a heading; every heading had three bullets. Completeness was the problem. A person makes a deck by deciding what not to say. A short post I read described this as covering everything, and it named what I had been feeling. The fix had to be upstream of layout.

designIntent.purpose: Name the texture as an absence of focus, not a visual style.
keep: No invented research claim; the observation stays personal
designIntent.requestedChange: Story-driven revision for the English introduction.

visibleText: The texture is not a style. It is an absence of focus.
A deck that tries to cover everything leaves the audience nothing to hold.

Every point gets a slide.
Every slide gets a heading.
Every heading gets three bullets.
Nothing is allowed to be the point.

title: The folder is the deck.
pages.notes: So I reversed the order. I don't ask for a deck and then write the talk. I talk first: why this exists, what I saw, what I decided, where I'm unsure. The model organizes that into a story, and we build pages from it. The Story field in the editor is where that intent lives for each page. The important part is not the feature; it's the direction of the work. The person supplies the point; the model helps with the form.

title: Two edits should not leave three decks.
pages.notes: Story-first only works if the document can keep up. When I tried to edit a real deck with an agent, two walls appeared. The first was mechanical. On a fifty-page deck, I'd ask for two pages to change. I'd get a new file. Then another. Defensive agents preserve instead of replace. The folder filled with near-duplicates and final versions, and I couldn't tell which one was the deck. Git had already solved this for code. The unit of change should be the page.

designIntent.purpose: Make the copy problem concrete: two changed pages arrive as another whole deck.
keep: The file list is a labeled sketch, not screenshot evidence
designIntent.requestedChange: Story-driven revision for the English introduction.

visibleText: Two edits should not leave three decks.
On a fifty-page talk, asking an agent to fix two pages often returns a new file, then another. The folder fills with near-duplicates, and the history lives in the file names.
The page is the unit of change.

title: The page is not a picture.
pages.notes: The second wall was the interface. With PowerPoint or Google Slides, the agent works through the screen. To judge a page it takes a full screenshot and looks at the picture. That is a bad loop: slow, expensive, and impossible to diff. You can't ask which object moved, or check bounds, or test a revision. Visual review still matters — a person still has to look — but it cannot be the only channel. I wanted the page to have a structure the agent could address directly.

designIntent.purpose: Show why screenshot-only review is a poor agent interface while keeping visual review necessary.
keep: Real page capture, not a mocked screen
designIntent.requestedChange: Story-driven revision for the English introduction.

visibleText: The page is not a picture.
An agent can target one text object, image or table, check its bounds, and diff the change. A screenshot is still how I judge composition; it is not the whole document.

title: PPTD plus React, in a desktop editor.
pages.notes: That led me to the file format. PowerPoint already keeps slides as separate parts inside the .pptx package; I'm not claiming it has no structure. But the structure is packed inside one file and the working interface is the screen. I wanted the slide to be a page in a folder: a manifest, one file per page, media beside it, history underneath. That's PPTD. I first met the idea in the Kimi Slides ecosystem; the open-source open-slide project gave me pages as React components. HUANDENG is the two things put together in an Electron editor. It is not a renamed PPTX.

designIntent.purpose: Explain the page-as-file model and credit open-slide without claiming PPTX has no structure.

Do not call HUANDENG an unpacked PPTX

title: A page can carry real evidence.
pages.notes: This is the scientific worked example: the Dickerson–Drew DNA dodecamer, PDB 1BNA. The plot measures C1′–C1′ distances at twelve paired positions within one deposited structure. It is not an experiment run by HUANDENG, not independent replicates, and not a set of hydrogen-bond lengths. The chart is an original measured figure kept in the asset library; the structure is drawn from the same coordinates. On the next page, this page's Story says what an edit must preserve.

title: Story tells the agent what to keep.
pages.notes: Story is stored with the page. A prompt disappears when the chat ends; this doesn't. It records what the page is for, what must not change, and what this edit is meant to do. When another agent — or another person — opens the page, they start from the intent, not from a guess. It's an alignment tool, not a guarantee. The model can still get it wrong; but at least it's wrong against something explicit.

designIntent.purpose: Make Story persistent: purpose and constraints live beside the page, not in chat.
designIntent.requestedChange: Story-driven revision for the English introduction.

title: One requested change, reviewed.
pages.notes: And when a change comes in, I can see the diff before I accept it. Not a chat message saying 'improved the slide', but the exact fields that changed, with the page's Story beside it. That turns review into something I can actually do. A diff is a better conversation than 'make it better'.

title: A page keeps its name when it moves.
pages.notes: This is the identity problem. If I tell an agent to change page four, and the order has changed since the last version, page four is a different page. So every page has a stable Slide ID — the four-character code — separate from its Position. In this real footer the page moved from position two to position four; the ID stayed C014. That means I can ask for C014, and the history belongs to C014 no matter where it sits.

designIntent.purpose: Separate Position from Slide ID with the real before/after footer evidence.
keep: Same page C014 in both strips
designIntent.requestedChange: Story-driven revision for the English introduction.

visibleText: A page keeps its name when it moves.
Position is where a page sits today. Slide ID is what it is.
The page moved two places. The ID did not. An agent can be asked for C014, not 'page four'.

title: History belongs to the page.
pages.notes: History is per page. Each page has named versions for the moments worth keeping, and an operation history for the smaller saves. Restoring a version changes only that page. That is the Git idea, applied at the unit that actually changes. I don't need a copy of the whole deck to try a different title.

designIntent.purpose: Show per-page named versions and the scope of restore.
keep: No claim that every keystroke is a version
designIntent.requestedChange: Story-driven revision for the English introduction.

visibleText: Two named versions. The older one can be read before it is restored. Restoring changes only this page.

title: Browse the deck. Read the argument.
pages.notes: These are the views around the canvas. Browse groups pages by Section and shows the stable Slide ID under each thumbnail. Outline is a reading view: title, a short Story summary, and the ID, so I can check the argument before opening a page. Sections edits the shared chapter structure; Notes gives a wide page for the talk; History is per page. They are peer views over one Main deck, not separate documents. The captures are from the public example project.

title: One source, many audiences.
pages.notes: One source, many talks. Main Slides is the canonical deck. A Presentation is a selection and order of those pages, with notes for that room. I can give a short version and a long version without maintaining two decks. If a page is fixed, every talk that uses it moves forward. If a talk has to stay exactly as it was, I can pin a version.

title: A library, not a pasteboard.
pages.notes: The materials library is the part I use most. Assets are stored once, at their original size, with their source and usage. This figure is a real one: C1′–C1′ distances at twelve paired positions in PDB 1BNA, one public structure. They are not independent replicates, and not hydrogen-bond distances; I use them as an example of real evidence, not as a result of the editor. The figure is referenced, not re-pasted, so the labels and pixels survive.

designIntent.purpose: Make the materials library real: assets stored once, referenced, with source and usage; show a real scientific figure.
designIntent.requestedChange: Story-driven revision for the English introduction.

visibleText: Assets are stored once, indexed by name and usage, and referenced by pages. A figure can move between pages without being pasted again.
The asset library and the page library are separate. “Unused” means not referenced by current Main pages, not safe to delete. Search by original filename, check usage, then jump to the page.

title: Several assistants, one shared writer.
pages.notes: This is the collaboration page. Codex and Claude Code use the local plugin; ChatGPT reaches the local editor through the authorized workstation route; DeepSeek Harness mounts the bundle. They share one writer, so different pages can be saved independently, but two edits to the same page conflict even if they touch different objects. Project Story, Sections and order share a metadata revision. Activity shows declared stages and saved receipts, not live presence or an automatic section lock. A content-to-design handoff works through saved operations and revisions: read the saved state, then preview, apply and render the focused change.
visibleText: Codex and Claude Code load the local plugin; ChatGPT uses the authorized workstation route; DeepSeek Harness mounts the bundle. Every write goes through the editor's shared writer and revision check.
Parallel by page, not by magic. No automatic section lock, scheduler or online presence. ChatGPT needs the authorized local route.

title: The work leaves as slides.
pages.notes: The work still has to leave the editor. PDF for the room. Editable PPTX for whoever has to keep it. MP4 when the deck has to play itself. Export reads the saved pages, not a screenshot of the editor, and the PPTX is a real editable file, not a folder of slide images. The format is a working format, not a lock-in.

designIntent.purpose: Close the loop: PDF, editable PPTX and MP4 from the saved pages.

title: A deck should sound like the person who made it.
pages.notes: That's the whole project. Not a better PowerPoint, and not a machine that makes decks for you. A way to start from the thing you actually want to say, and keep the document close enough to the person that it still sounds like them. The next step is more direct manipulation — layers, the kind of editing you do in an image tool — but the order is the point. Story first; slides after.
